findings.text: Message queue creation or lookup service takes a key and flag word, resolves the caller IPC namespace from current context, packages them as parameters with queue creation and association callbacks, and delegates to a generic get routine.

Message queue control service validates that identifier and command are non-negative, resolves the caller namespace, then dispatches info, status, set, and remove operations; status and set translate between user and kernel descriptor forms with a version selector, while set and remove pass through a down path.
Legacy control entry parses a version bit out of the command word and then invokes the same control implementation with the derived version, preserving old user layout handling.

Identifier allocator initializes reference count, clamps limit, arms preload, initializes and acquires object guard, stamps owner and creator identities from current credentials, clears deletion state, allocates index and sequence, links non-private keys into a hash, tracks usage and high index, and on failure marks deleted and releases guards.
Generic get dispatcher selects private creation path when key equals private, otherwise selects public lookup-or-create path.

Public lookup holds the identifier set write guard during find and optional create, returns not-found when absent without create, returns exists when create plus exclusive collides, otherwise runs optional extra checks and permission plus association checks before releasing object and set guards.

Permission evaluator audits the object, folds flag bits into a three-bit request, selects owner, group, or other grant by shifting stored mode according to identity or group membership, denies when requested bits exceed grant without owner capability in the namespace, otherwise defers to a security permission hook.

Control lookup for set and remove obtains the object by identifier, audits it and for set also audits proposed ownership and mode plus extra limit, then permits only owner, creator, or namespace administrator capability, returning a permission error otherwise.
Reference release decrements the object count and only when it reaches zero schedules deferred reclamation through read-copy-update with a caller supplied free callback.

Permission update converts supplied user and group identifiers in current user namespace, rejects invalid mappings, then replaces stored owner and group and updates only permission bits of mode while preserving other mode bits.

Kernel to user permission translation copies key, mode, and sequence verbatim and converts four identity fields through munged mapping in current user namespace; reverse translation copies key, mode, sequence, and identities with set macros.
Version parser treats presence of a 64-bit flag in the command as new layout and clears that flag, otherwise selects old layout.
Group membership test reports true when the queried group equals the current filesystem group, otherwise searches the credential supplementary group list.
Group identifier display mapping translates a kernel group identifier upward through the target namespace map and substitutes a global overflow value when unmappable.

New queue starts with mode masked to permission bits, caller key, cleared security hook state, zero send and receive times, current real time as change time, zero byte and message counts, namespace default capacity, cleared last sender and receiver pids, and three empty lists for messages, receivers, and senders.
A send fits only when both its size plus current bytes stays within capacity and current count plus one stays within capacity; capacity therefore bounds both bytes and count.

Identifier index allocation prefers cyclic reuse bounded by usage-derived and configured limits, increments a sequence on wrap past the last index with wrap to zero at a configured maximum, stores sequence in the object, publishes the pointer, and composes the user visible identifier from sequence shifted plus index; restore path instead decodes sequence and index from supplied identifier.

Non-private keys are inserted into a key hash after index allocation; hash insertion failure removes the index and propagates the error, and any allocation failure marks the object deleted before releasing guards.

Old status export zero fills the destination, converts permission, copies three timestamps, saturates byte, message, and capacity counts at 16-bit maximum while also providing full values in extended fields, and copies last sender and receiver pids; new export copies the full structure.

Old control input copies only owner, group, mode, and capacity, selecting extended capacity when the short capacity field is zero; new input copies the full descriptor and faults propagate as input-output errors.

Info query always reports namespace limits and two compile-time size constants, reports live usage for one command variant and fixed historical constants for the other, and returns the highest index or zero when empty; the result buffer is zeroed first to avoid exposing padding.

Status query selects lookup by position for two variants and validated lookup by identifier for classic status, enforces read permission except for the any variant which only audits, validates security policy, rechecks deletion under lock, then reports permission, timestamps with high halves on 32-bit, usage, capacity, and numeric last pids, returning zero for classic status and full identifier for the other variants.
Validity is defined solely as deletion flag clear; permission and deletion rechecks occur while holding the object guard.
Pid field update replaces the stored reference only when different, acquiring the new reference before dropping the old one.
Maximum index reporting returns negative one when empty, configured maximum minus one when full, otherwise the stored high index.

Allocation initializes and acquires the object spin guard under read-copy-update read lock and returns with both held on success; caller must release object guard then read lock. Lookup by key also returns with both held. Combined helpers release object guard alone or object guard plus read lock.

Creation and public lookup paths serialize on the identifier set write guard; info path uses the read guard; control down path holds write guard across the whole operation plus read lock during lookup and object guard for mutation.

Removal and set paths acquire object guard after control lookup, mutate under it, queue wakeups while holding it, release object guard before delivering wakeups, and finally release read and write guards in defined order; teardown additionally releases read lock after wakeup delivery before freeing queued messages.

Permission header carries linkage for deferred free, a spin guard, reference count, key, user visible identifier, sequence, owner, group, creator user and group, mode, deletion flag, hash node, and opaque security state.

Queue object embeds the permission header and adds send, receive, and change timestamps, current bytes, current message count, capacity limit, last sender and receiver pid references, and three list heads for queued messages, waiting receivers, and waiting senders.
Identifier set carries a read-write guard, usage count, high index, last index, sequence counter, optional restore next identifier, an identifier tree, and a key hash table.

Blocked sender record carries a waiting task reference, requested message size, and queue linkage; blocked receiver record carries a waiting task reference, a result pointer updated with release ordering, and queue linkage.

Sender wait lifecycle enqueues current task as interruptible at tail, removes on cancellation only if still linked, and on wakeup scans in order: forced kill mode detaches linkage and queues every waiter, normal mode stops after one full pass without progress and rotates unfit waiters to tail while queueing only those whose request now fits.

Receiver abort walks all waiting receivers, takes a task reference, publishes an encoded error result with release semantics, and queues a safe wakeup; removal uses a removed-identifier error while permission change uses a retry error.

Teardown transitions a queue from live to deleted, aborts receivers and senders into a wake queue, unlinks accounting, releases guards, delivers wakeups, then frees each queued message with header and byte accounting, clears last pid references, and drops the final reference toward deferred free.

Control down either removes the queue through teardown or updates permission and capacity: capacity growth beyond namespace default requires resource capability, then under object guard it stamps change time, aborts receivers that may have lost access, and wakes newly eligible senders.

Object becomes visible to lockless lookup as soon as its pointer is published, so it must be fully initialized before publication and every publication failure must follow full teardown of deletion marking, reference drop, and deferred free.

Wakeups are collected while holding the object guard and delivered only after releasing it, avoiding waking tasks that would immediately block on the same guard; sender scan relies on that guard for ordering without extra barriers.
Receiver result publication uses release ordering paired with a barrier read elsewhere, so pairing must be preserved when reimplementing the handoff.
Identifier sequence shift is supplied by one of two definitions depending on build configuration, and maximum sequence is the largest signed integer shifted right by that amount.

User descriptor selection uses two version tags where the 64-bit tag may be embedded in the command word; old layout uses 16-bit saturated counters plus extended full-width fields and a zero-selects-extended rule for capacity.
